identification.summary: Microsoft tracks Storm-0249 as an access broker active since 2021 that distributes at least BazaLoader, IcedID, Bumblebee and Emotet [S1]. Reporting states it sells footholds in victim networks to other cybercrime groups, including ransomware and extortion actors [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Active since 2021 per Microsoft [S1]. The Hacker News states Microsoft first highlighted the group in September 2024; the underlying Microsoft document was not located [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-0249. Malpedia lists DEV-0249 as a synonym [S5]. Secondary sources say it supplied access to Storm-0501 [S2][S5]; the Microsoft tax-season post retrieved does not mention this [S1]. Bumblebee operators are tracked separately by Google TAG as EXOTIC LILY per secondary reporting; do not merge them with Storm-0249.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified in the sources gathered. Described as a financially motivated initial access broker serving ransomware and extortion actors [S1][S2][S3].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the 6 February 2025 tax-themed campaign to Storm-0249 by name [S1]. ReliaQuest attributes the later EDR-abuse activity to Storm-0249; that is a vendor assessment, not Microsoft's [S3].
attribution.basis: Microsoft campaign analysis and indicators [S1]; ReliaQuest investigation of ClickFix, MSI and DLL sideloading activity [S3][S2].

objectives: Financial gain by gaining and selling persistent access to compromised networks to ransomware affiliates, shortening the time from intrusion to encryption [S3][S2].

sectors: Engineering, IT and consulting (tax-themed campaign second wave; this wave was reported alongside Storm-0249's February 2025 activity) [S6]
targeting.notes: Microsoft attributes only the 6 February 2025 campaign to Storm-0249; that campaign sent several thousand IRS/tax-themed emails to US users [S1]. A second February 2025 wave reaching over 2,300 US organizations was reported in the same Microsoft post by secondary coverage, but Microsoft attributes only the first campaign to this actor [S1][S6]. Victim sectors for the EDR-abuse activity are not stated in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Historic loader distribution: BazaLoader, IcedID, Bumblebee, Emotet [S1]. February 2025: PDF lure with DoubleClick redirect through Rebrandly to a fake DocuSign page, with system and IP filtering, then a Firebase-hosted JavaScript file that installs Brute Ratel C4 and Latrodectus (v1.9) via MSI [S1]. Researchers report later use of ClickFix and fake-captcha lures delivered from compromised WordPress sites [S7]. ReliaQuest reports ClickFix lures leading victims to run curl in the Windows Run dialog, fetching an MSI that runs with SYSTEM privileges, drops a legitimate SentinelOne executable plus a trojanized DLL in AppData (the specific filename SentinelAgentWorker.exe was not confirmed in primary sources), uses fileless PowerShell, spoofed Microsoft-look-alike domains, and C2 through the signed process [S2][S3]. ReliaQuest says this is not a SentinelOne vulnerability and could apply to other EDR products [S2][S3].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-0249 as an access broker active since 2021 distributing BazaLoader, IcedID, Bumblebee and Emotet.

campaigns.name: First Microsoft highlight
campaigns.summary: The Hacker News states Microsoft first highlighted the group in September 2024; primary Microsoft document not located.

campaigns.name: Tax-themed phishing delivering BRc4 and Latrodectus
campaigns.summary: Several thousand IRS-themed emails to US users: PDF, DoubleClick and Rebrandly redirect, fake DocuSign page, filtered delivery of a JavaScript file that installs Brute Ratel C4 then Latrodectus. Microsoft published indicators on 2025-04-03.

campaigns.name: ClickFix / fake-captcha hunting reports
campaigns.summary: A defender blog reports Storm-0249 using fake-captcha (ClickFix) techniques and compromised WordPress sites for lures. Only seen via search snippet.

campaigns.name: EDR process abuse reported by ReliaQuest
campaigns.summary: ReliaQuest reports a shift from mass phishing to targeted ClickFix, MSI and DLL sideloading via a legitimate SentinelOne executable, with pre-profiled access passed to ransomware affiliates.

diamond.adversary: Access broker tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0249; financially motivated; sells access to ransomware and extortion actors [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Phishing and ClickFix social engineering, Brute Ratel C4, Latrodectus, MSI droppers, DLL sideloading into a signed EDR binary, fileless PowerShell [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Rebrandly shortener, fake DocuSign page, Firebase-hosted script, and BRc4 and Latrodectus C2 domains listed by Microsoft [S1]; spoofed Microsoft-look-alike domains and C2 routed through the EDR process per ReliaQuest [S2][S3]; compromised WordPress sites per a defender blog [S7].
diamond.victim: US users and organizations targeted with tax lures in 2025 [S1]; downstream victims are ransomware targets served by buyers of the access [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cybercrime access-brokerage economy supplying ransomware affiliates [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, user-run commands via the Run dialog, trusted EDR processes and signed binaries, and email and document-signing brand trust [S1][S3].

gaps: Primary Microsoft document for the September 2024 highlight and the Storm-0501 link was not found; only secondary coverage [S2][S5].
ReliaQuest original report and The Hacker News article could not be fetched (hosts unreachable); details come from search-result summaries and the title [S2][S3].
Exact publication date of the ReliaQuest report is not verified; December 2025 inferred from secondary URL path [S2][S3].
Victim names, sectors and named ransomware buyers for the EDR-abuse activity are not public in gathered sources.
Defender blog on fake-captcha TTPs and Malpedia profile were seen only via search snippets, not opened [S5][S7].
Whether the tax-themed campaign and the EDR-abuse activity are the same operators beyond vendor attribution is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is user endpoints and the trusted EDR agent process; the battlespace includes email and web channels reaching DoD-adjacent contractor staff. STEP 2: Brokers shorten the gap between initial access and ransomware, so dwell time before encryption may be days [S3]. STEP 3: Template is lure (tax-themed PDF or ClickFix), MSI, sideloaded DLL in a signed binary, C2 disguised as agent telemetry, then handoff of access [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued sale of access to ransomware affiliates against commercial targets, including defense industrial base firms by opportunity. MDCOA is the same tradecraft tailored to other EDR products against cleared contractors, giving criminal or proxy buyers a foothold in sensitive networks. Candidate indicators: curl.exe or reg.exe launched by security agents, signed EDR binaries loading DLLs from AppData, EDR processes contacting newly registered domains, Run-dialog command execution, and the Microsoft-published domains and hashes [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track broker-to-ransomware handoff reporting; early detection of broker footholds is a warning of impending extortion. (2) Authorities: DIB and contractor incident reporting and DC3 coordination apply; confirm applicable authorities for any response on non-DoD networks. (3) Mission assurance: do not assume the EDR agent is trustworthy; add behavioral baselines for agent network and child-process activity and hunt for sideloading. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the DIB CS program and vendors; vendor attribution is not government attribution [S1][S3].
